newsitem.title: SPAIN: Peseta shrugs off rate cut, seen stable at 84/84.55.
newsitem.headline: Peseta shrugs off rate cut, seen stable at 84/84.55.

text.p: Despite a modest, initial correction on Tuesday after the Bank of Spain sanctioned its third rate cut in the year, the peseta is stable and dealers expect it to trade sideways between 84.00 and 84.55 per mark in the coming months.
As the Spanish central bank announced a 25 basis points cut in its key money rate to 5.50 percent, the peseta slid to around 84.22/25 per mark versus 84.12/14 at the close on Monday.
But financial experts said the rate decision, widely expected, would not affect the Spanish currency any further.
They added that the peseta is likely to react more to the mood on Europe's single currency.

"With this cut we'll see a very tight range for the peseta, between 84.15/55, with the Bank of Spain vigilant on whether it gets weaker or stronger," said Juan Antonio Mielgo economist with Bank of America in Madrid.
After March data showed the consumer price index (CPI) up 2.2 percent year on year from 2.5 percent in February, monetary easing was largely discounted by the market.

"Really the rate cut will not have so many consequences short run. It could leave the peseta more reactive if Europessimism should return. We could seen it moving faster to around 85 (per mark)," said Cesar Cantalapietra, economist at Analistas Financieros Internacional (AFI) in Madrid.
Positive economic fundamentals and a rising dollar are seen supporting the peseta, short run, while fat currency reserves at the Bank of Spain should further cushion the unit's stability.

"In two to three months the peseta is likely to remain strong between 84 and 84.50 per mark. From one side the dollar is likely to stay high versus the mark, from the other Spain's economy is recovering," said Fernando Mazon, analyst at Adisa Catalunya.
The Bank of Spain, having heavily bought pesetas in February and March when the Spanish currency was approaching the 85 per mark, is now seen on hold.

"We think the Bank of Spain has a target to keep the peseta between its central parity at 85.07 per mark and a 2.25 percent stronger, just above 83.00 per mark," said Antonio Villaroya, analyst of Merrill Lynch in Madrid.
The Bank of Spain's easing was seen as cautious, an attitude which was also supportive of the peseta.

"The peseta was not really affected by today's cut. The Bank of Spain has proved to be very cautious in its cuts. Both in March and at the moment fundamentals would have allowed it to cut by 50 basis points. Given this moderation the peseta is reacting very well," said Merill Lynch's Villarroya.
Longer term the peseta is seen influenced by progress toward the European Monetary Union.

"We'll depend on official remarks on the Euro. The recent recovery was mainly due to the Ecofin meeting," said Mazon. "But if tensions or doubts come back, the peseta will slide at least 50 points, back to around 84.50/85,00."
"Now (the European outlook) is neutral, maybe a bit optimistic. But this can change very fast, at any moment," said Villarroya.
